opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think hardware is definitely a real factor, but in my view it's probably not the main bottleneck right now. If you look at what current robot hardware can already do when it's teleoperated by a skilled human, it's actually remarkably capable. You can have someone remotely control a fairly inexpensive arm and get it to fold laundry, cook, tidy up a table, a lot of the dexterous tasks we'd love robots to do autonomously. So the physical capability is, to a large degree, already there. What's missing is the intelligence, the software that can figure out what to do in a new environment, generalize to objects it hasn't seen, and recover when things go wrong.

That said, there are places where hardware does hold us back. Tactile sensing is one. Humans rely enormously on touch when we manipulate things, and most robots today have very limited or very noisy touch sensing, so they're doing a lot with vision alone. Hands are another. Building robust, dexterous, multi-fingered hands that are also cheap and don't break constantly is still really hard. And then there's cost and reliability in general. If a robot costs a lot and needs frequent repairs, it's hard to deploy many of them, and that limits how much data you can collect, which then feeds back into the learning problem.

So I'd say hardware and learning are coupled. Better, cheaper hardware lets you gather more data and run more experiments, and better learning algorithms let you get more out of imperfect hardware. But if I had to point to where the biggest gap is today, it's on the algorithmic side: how we build models that can reason, plan, and compose knowledge to handle situations they weren't explicitly trained on. That's a lot of what I focus on in my own work, things like using generative models and energy-based models to let robots plan and generalize compositionally, rather than just memorizing behaviors from demonstrations.

r001.rationale: It says a skilled human can remotely control a robot to “cook” and perform other dexterous tasks, indicating existing robots can handle a broad range of tasks under remote control.

r002.rationale: It discusses how better, cheaper hardware can enable more data collection and how learning and hardware are coupled, but does not argue that successful autonomous AI would increase interest in developing better hardware.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think hardware is actually a pretty significant bottleneck, but maybe not in the way people usually frame it. The common story is that the robots themselves are bad, that the arms aren't precise enough or the hands don't have enough degrees of freedom. And there's some truth to that, especially on the dexterity side. If you look at a human hand, we have very rich tactile sensing, we have compliance, we can do all these in-hand manipulation things. Most robot hands today are either parallel-jaw grippers or these very expensive, fragile multi-fingered hands that break constantly. So for a lot of the tasks we'd actually want robots to do in a home, the morphology is just limiting what's even possible to learn.

But I'd say the bigger issue from a learning perspective is the data side, and that's really a hardware problem in disguise. In language and vision, we got these huge gains because there's essentially infinite data sitting on the internet. For robotics, every data point requires a physical robot moving in the physical world, in real time. You can't speed that up, and robots are expensive, they wear out, they need people supervising them. So the amount of real robot data that exists is tiny compared to what we're used to in other domains, and that constrains how far you can push the scaling story.

That's part of why I've been interested in approaches that try to get around this, things like learning world models or generative models from video, where you can leverage data that wasn't collected on a robot at all, and then use the robot primarily for grounding and fine-tuning. Simulation is another route, though the sim-to-real gap is still very real, especially for contact-rich manipulation.

And then there's the compute side, which people talk about less. If you want to run a large model on a robot that has to react in tens of milliseconds, you can't always just call out to a giant cluster. So there's a real question of how much reasoning you can do on-board versus what latency you can tolerate, and that shapes which algorithms are actually practical.

So overall, I'd say hardware isn't the single thing holding robotics back, but it's deeply entangled with the data problem, and I think progress will come from co-designing the learning methods around those constraints rather than waiting for the hardware to get good enough.

r001.rationale: The response discusses robot-hand limitations and home tasks, but does not say robots can perform a broad range of kitchen tasks under remote human control.

r002.rationale: It says progress depends on co-designing learning methods around hardware constraints, but does not argue that successful autonomous AI demonstrations would spur interest in better hardware.

astra-6.text:
I think hardware is part of the story, but I don’t think it’s the main bottleneck right now. We already have robots that can execute quite precise movements. If you have a person teleoperate one, you can get it to do fairly complicated tasks. That suggests there’s a lot more we could get out of the existing hardware if we had better intelligence controlling it.

The challenge is getting a robot to act autonomously in a new situation—to understand what’s happening, decide what to do, and recover when something goes wrong. Hardware improvements certainly help, especially in reliability, dexterity, and cost. But I think there’s still substantial room for progress on the software side before we hit the limits of what today’s hardware can do.

r001.rationale: It says teleoperated robots can perform “fairly complicated tasks,” but does not specify kitchen tasks or a broad range of them.

r002.rationale: It says better intelligence could make more use of existing hardware, but does not argue that autonomous AI success would increase interest in developing better hardware.

sol-6.1.text:
I think hardware is part of the challenge, but I wouldn’t say it’s the main thing holding robotics back. We already have robots that can execute fairly precise motions. What’s much harder is getting them to understand a new situation and reliably decide what to do, especially outside a controlled environment.

Hardware does affect how quickly we can make progress, though. Robots are expensive, they wear down, and collecting real-world experience takes time. You can’t scale that as easily as training on text or images. So better, cheaper, more reliable hardware would help enormously, particularly with data collection. But there’s still a substantial intelligence problem to solve with the hardware we have today.

r001.rationale: The response says robots can execute fairly precise motions, but does not claim they can perform a broad range of kitchen tasks under remote human control.

r002.rationale: The response says better hardware would help and that robotics still has an intelligence problem; it does not say successful autonomous AI demonstrations would increase interest in better hardware.
